en: The Amoghānandinī Instruction:
Now I shall proclaim the instruction that brings about unfailing joy;
by the mere hearing of which one becomes victorious everywhere. 1
The labials, the dentals, the short [vowel], and again that which has a short vowel following it—these characteristics, together with the resonance (nāda) and the nasal (nāsikya), are each distinct.
"O Brahma-arms, firmly bound, O Great One, bind the sky! he who [binds].
O Bṛhaspati, shining upon the sacrificial grass, protect us and awaken us to much;
drink with the sacrificial grass, they say, for the sake of those whose intellects are oppressed by Tryambaka;
may the kinsman and the supporter bind [us] together with Ambikā for the sake of the tawny one. 4.
He said: "O Ṛbāsi, O Bambhāra, and Amba as well, Babhu and Bahu—the embryo of the Kṣatriya, as well as Abda and Śatabasti, are abandoned by the wise.
One should not omit the first syllable; one should avoid the second."
Thus, with many [strands] upon his arms, he should abandon Pūrṇabandhu.
As he bears it, I speak to him who bears the water-bearing hole:
let the tawny one seize the bond and the seed from the sin of the fetter.
When you were at the head of the host, Agni, armed with arrows,
woke up; he who was bound for the sake of the helmeted one, like Bilmin,
shattered Kubala and Vibala as well as their army.
The power that destroys the Rākṣasas is to be relinquished; the final labial is called "power" (bala).
It is considered to be joined with these: the semivowels, the letter *ya*, and the letter *va*.
[One] abandons Arbuda, Nyarbuda, Babhru, Śulba, and Ulba.
And speak much that is loathsome; O Bhaḍavā, holding the pillar!
O Ambike, ambe, ambālike, balāyakā!
O Ambike, baṣkihā, drive away the outsider from the sacrificial grass!
Even though they have forgotten the Veda and the Varas, I shall declare these to you:
Vidalkārī for the eunuch, Jumbaka for the bound, Śābalyā for the loathsome, and Āḍambarā for the sound. 12–13.
And "baṇ mahām̐śca," "baḍ āditya," and "baṭ sūryasya subīraye"—in whose verses we declare this abundantly, and which [the text] maintains;
you maintain, you maintain for praise, according to the sequence in the *Saṃhitā*. 14.
These are declared to be labials; the remaining ones are proclaimed to be dentals.
Viṣṇu, Vāyu, as well as Agni, the piercing heat of Varuṇa, and that of Vasu—these eight shine forth for the universe, and they are proclaimed to be dentals. 15–16.
"Vāmam adya vināścaiva, vṛṣabhas tathā vṛśīnām,
badhyamānaś ca vṛtraṃ ca, vācaḥ satyam aśīya ca.
(17) "vṛṣṇo vamyro vadho 'sīti," and "vapā urvīṃ vahanti ca."
Veda, barcca, and varāha— these are proclaimed as the dentals (18).
Valo, vasti, vala, vāhana, burīta, vivabru, kubala, vibala, cāpa, and arbāṇa— these ten are said to be dentals (19).
*vakṣi*, *mukṣva*, and likewise *vakṣyamāṇam*— whatever such forms may be—
as well as *vyetvā*, *vyītām*, and similarly *vyanta*, *uṣe*, and *yahvī*, these are declared to be *pīḍyahasta*. (20)
*vviśalyo*, *vāṇī*, and these two *vṛṣṇa* are proclaimed as dental.
We know *te*, *vibhṛteḥ*, *cetau*, *pratadvaḥ*, and *cet* belong to the dental class; likewise, *vittasya*, *vibhrāṣṭi*, *vibhrāṭ*, and *vibhrājamānā* are recorded by the wise as dentals. 21–22.
Not so, O Goddesses; the Goddess indeed sustains it thus.
He shattered that power which slays the Rākṣasas and is formidable; likewise, Jātavedas [shattered] the Sāmaveda. Nine times you do not die.
The wind blows after the leaf-eating birds that are eager for food; these teeth are powerful like arrows, and their strength is firm—there is never any doubt about this.
Likewise, in a *saṃhitā*, the syllables indeed become light. 24–25.
When the single syllable *va* occurs as a particle (*nipāta*) in *saṃhitā*, it becomes light; at the time of the *pada-pāṭha*, it becomes heavy.
The syllable *va* is said to be of three kinds: heavy, light, and lighter.
If the letter *va* is seen at the end of a word or in the middle of a word, it should be considered light;
indeed, even elsewhere, it is lighter still. (27–28)

When the syllable *au* occurs as a preceding word and the syllable *a* follows it, one should recognize the fire-in-fire illustration as being even more subtle. These sounds— ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, and m— are known by the technical term "nasals" (*anunāsika*).
Those vowels which occur in conjunction with semivowels (*antasthā*) within a *pratyaya*,
as well as the letter *ha* and the third and fourth letters of the consonant classes (*varga*), along with the long vowels ending in the *visarga*— these eight are designated as *nāda*. 30–31.
Where there are two *m*s at the beginning and end and a *h* in the middle, one should produce the *nāda* there; "O Agni, Lord of Vows" (*agne vratapate*) is the illustration.
When the first word ends in *m* and the subsequent [word] begins with *a*, [the *nāda* is produced]. 32.
In that regard, one should produce a resonance (*nāda*); "like a fly" is the illustration.
The *guru* consonants known as *nāda*, as well as the *laghu* nasals, conjuncts, and the *visarga*—these are proclaimed to be resonant (*nāda*). (33–34)
Where the fifth [vowel] is seen when another fifth follows, one should apply the *nāsikya* there by way of a *mātrā*; of this there is no doubt.
At the end of a conjunct consonant there is a pause, and especially so at the point of a *vivṛtti*.
Those which are voiceless (aghoṣa) consonants following a vowel, as well as the fifth vowels [nasalized], when joined at the end of a word—these five short vowels are indeed nasalized (anunāsika).
They occur in the opening [of a word] or at the pause (avasāna), and likewise others in the middle of a half-verse (ṛc-ardha). 36–37.

Wherever the letter *ya* is seen joined with either a short (*kṣipra*) or a long (*dīrgha*) vowel, it is prescribed as the *nāsikya* (nasalized) when situated at the end of a word or within a quarter-verse (*pāda*). Furthermore, when a word ending in *ka* precedes and the vowel *ṛ* follows, [the same applies].
One should know that "nāsika" (nasal) refers to the letter *ṇa*; this is the illustration. The letter *ha*, joined with *repha* (*ra*), is always without *nāda* (vowel resonance);
even when stepped upon by the second [letter], it never possesses *nāda*. 39–40.
Where they destroy the enemies, the ritual acts, the trees, and the enclosing sticks— the enemies who do not move away—
there the five *anuraṅga* vowels become one-and-a-half-mora units.
Pūṣan, Mitra, and Vasu are proclaimed as the *añjana* [vowels].
Having remained for one half-measure, these five nasalized [consonants] arise;
the five colors proceed from the Vajrin who destroys and annihilates.
One should know *ahiṇaḥ* and *prahiṇo*; the illustrations are like *ī*, *ū*, and *ṝ*. 42–43.

"Devām̐ 2 | āsādaya" is the *ghāta*. "Devām̐ 2 | iḍeṣi" is the *nirghāta*. "Devām̐ 2 upāgā" belongs to the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*). "Devām̐ 2 ṛtubhiḥ" belongs to the serpent (*ahi*). "Amitrām̐ 2 oṣatāt" belongs to the one who sends forth (*prāhin*). Whether consisting of two morae or even one, when it rests upon the root of the nose, the *raṅga* is employed at the end with all five nasal sounds. 44
"Baṭ," "mahām̐śca," "baḍādityo," "hyaddhā," and "devamahām̐"—these are proclaimed as the five great *raṅgas* (stages) of Sūrya.
Furthermore, "parite," "parimāgne," and "adṛśraṃ" are proclaimed [as others]. 45–46.
In which the non-dual [verses] are seen, proclaimed as the *atiraṅga*s:
"O Agni, 3, for the cooked [oblation], O Svar, 3, the parched grains, 3, the *śācī* [verses]"—this is repeated twice;
"the crosswise one is stretched out, I ask you, Vāyu, the wind"—these seven become *pluta*s, for an eighth does not exist. 46–47.

The mind-impulse (*manojūti*) and the wind (*vāyu*) constitute one *pluta* vowel which is divided into two; all *pluta* vowels beginning with the syllable *o* are likewise [divided], and there is never any doubt regarding this. (48) However, for the *jātya* and the *anupadha* types, the measure is six finger-breadths.
It may occupy only a fourth part [of the body], yet by that alone it continues to exist. Even a piśāca roars in an empty house but is not seen;
in this way the phonemes (varṇas) are to be employed—this is the illustration for the term "upajjman. 49-50.
The throbbing at the root of the chin, fully filled by the vital air, is called the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkasphuraṇa); it is the sign of the subsiding of phlegm. 51.
[Recite: *iḍe rante'śvinna kṛtasyate pātanno yaste yuvaṃ surāmam*.

"iḍa ehi. At the time of the word-division (*padakāla*) and in the sentence (*vākya*), however, there are five short vowels: *sarasvati*, two *ja*-sounds, and the letter *m*. Above that stands the letter *r*;
one should know this as the bodiless Yama. "I cleanse thoroughly" (*saṃmārjmi*) is the illustration.

"iyante dyāmmā suvīrān suprajāḥ prajāḥ | raśminā sattyāya | paro divā pṛthivyā" — these six end with the *svara* (accent) vowels. If one were to reduce the work to ashes like a blacksmith [by improper application], thus should the phonemes (*varṇas*) be employed for a year.
If one who has a copper-colored back recites the form of *ūṣman*, he is ordained [as such];
and if the wise man acts in this way, it is called "the auspicious one"— this is the illustration (nidarśana) 54–55.
Just as birds seeking fish fly up and swoop down, so too should the phonemes (varṇas) be employed; this is the view that they should be auspicious. 56.
Having abandoned the "tortoise-back" [mode of articulation], one should act like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
For thus does the one possessing supernormal knowledge (abhijña) demonstrate the "tvā" of the deity.
Or, like a cock greedy for meat, one should utter two "ka" sounds;
in this way the phonemes (varṇas) are to be employed—the cock is the illustration. 57–58.
The hen, greedy for food, repeatedly makes a clucking sound;
the wise man makes his face like that—this is the illustration of the cock (59).
Just as one burdened by a heavy load breathes with a light mind.
Thus the vowels (varṇas) are to be employed; this is the illustration for the Hotṛ priest.
Just as the breath of a young, small-minded serpent is subtle, so too should the *ūṣman* be employed, excluding the letter *ha*.

Just as a mother with a child kisses her face again and again out of affection, so does the wise man perform the visualization while practicing yoga. Just as a woman afflicted by passion makes such sounds as she does— 62. So too does the practitioner.
The wise man produces that sound; "siṃhyasi" is the illustration (63).
Just as the fight between two monkeys rushes forward with fury, so should the phonemes be employed; "kikidīvinā" is the illustration (64).

If the letter *u* is seen at the end of the word *mūtra* and also at the beginning of the word *yoni*, the wise man should form their union like the mouth of a fine drum; this is the illustration of the *sadundubhi*. (65)
One should know that *dvirauṣṭhya* (the double-lip articulation) is the illustration of *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
That which is produced with a single effort is called *sakṛdauṣṭhya*;
then follow *dvirauṣṭhya*, *trirauṣṭhya*, *caturauṣṭhya*, and beyond that, *pañcauṣṭhya*.
Now, that which is to be known through similarity between two [persons] of identical voice and complexion— one should designate those very eyes as "excessive" or "deficient.
Having addressed the Viśvedevas, he who at any time—
"O gods, let there be salutation to you; may strength come to us.

(RV 10.128.69) In the case of a conflict between identical vowels (*samānākṣara*), the *sandhi* [vowel] and the two eyes (*cakṣuṣī*) [are the solution]; and in the case of a combination of identical consonants (*samānavarṇa*), the two eyes are indeed the primary authorities. (70)
"May Mitra be gracious to us," likewise "the wind," "they declare him to be upright," and "mind in offspring and progeny"— these four [verses] constitute the eyes.
Having seen the first section (kaṇḍikā), the subsequent one is joined with a thousand.
That alone is the mention of the name; it is never a mere conceptual construction.
Where a *kaṇḍikā* is seen to be preceded by another and ending with another, that should be known as *capalā*; "āccha" is the illustration of its meter.
For there are three half-verses in "abhityam," three half-verses in "prajāpatiḥ punātu mā," four in "vāyuḥ," five thereafter,
three in "anāghṛṣṭā," and four half-verses in "edho'si."
"You are the year; there are four [syllables]; heaven is peace in two halves.

(75) In some cases one should pronounce "svāhā" separately, while in others one should join it; in some instances it should be known to come at the beginning, and in others it is prescribed at the end. (76)
One should cast the oblation at the time of the sentence, at its conclusion, or at the end of the word *svāhā*;
one should separate the portion of the mantra and utter the word *svāhā* separately. Furthermore, the sentence may begin with *svāhā*, as in the case of *nṛmaṇā* and *nṛmaṇas*.
At the beginning, in the middle, and again at the end, the visualization is "kāya svāhā.
The first *kaṇḍikā* is recorded as having eighty-one syllables; according to the methods stated in the definition, "iṣe tvā" is the illustrative example. 78–79.

Three, three, four, ten, five, and the eighth is remembered as having eleven syllables; likewise, this is seen for both [the *puraścaraṇa* and the *sādhana*]. The seventh and the fifth likewise again have eleven syllables.
One should know the nine-syllable [mantra], and the eleven-syllable is traditionally taught.
There is nothing higher than the high, and likewise nothing lower than the low;
thus should the phonemes (varṇas) be employed, as illustrated by the phrase "iṣe tvā. 81–82.
A sentence beginning with the letter *ma* is auspicious; woolen cloth (*ūrṇa*) is highly praised.
A sentence beginning with *ā*, *vi*, or *m* and ending with a vowel consists of the first vowels;
such a sentence may contain eleven or four syllables, repeated again and again.
The two pairs of arrows [ten], these two [two], seven at the end, and fourteen;
eighty-four is the measure of the syllables according to the five groups of five letters.
In the case of Indra and Āditya, it should be understood that his statement consists of three parts.
The first *adhyakṣā* is *sudhā*, while the second is *pīḍyādhyakṣā*.
The first should be known as ending in *ūṣman*; the other follows after the *armas*.
Between these two, there are correctly two *kaṇḍikās* for both *adhyakṣā*s.
From the word *abhi*, four [syllables] are prescribed for Agni;
furthermore, a single-syllable word and a sentence of nine, four, and two [syllables] are ordained.
There is a single-syllable word in the middle, and two [syllables] each at the beginning and the end of the verse.

Thus should the phonemes (varṇas) be employed; they have been proclaimed for the world. One should understand the word-ending with its case-suffix from the teacher and from the scriptures. This is the determination of sentences, whether by means of elision, augmentation, or modification. 89–90.
In the forests, he pervaded the mid-air; thus he manifested eight [names].
At the time of receiving the name, however, it is the guru alone who bestows them—of this there is no doubt. [The names are: Śarman, Sthas, Citra, Upaprāgāt, and Samuddrava.
At the time of forming a sentence, the *udātta* accent does not occur where a *svarita* is prescribed;
as in "ehy ū ṣu śukrā jāte" and "abhittvā gomad ūṣuṇā," at the time of forming a sentence, the *svarita* does not cause the hand to be raised upward. 92–93.

One should know the words "akṣan," "amīmadanta," and "ca," as well as "aharahaḥ" and likewise "tathā," and the *svarita* accent during recitation according to their sequence (verse 94). Furthermore, one should recognize where the *ūṣman* sounds and the *antastha* sounds appear.

In that very place, the Guru is to be known as being endowed with a thousand vowels (ṛ-varṇa). When there is a conjunction with internal words (antastha-pada), no further distinction arises. One should know Yama to be bodiless; the internal consonants (antastha) are the leaders of the clusters (piṇḍa). 95–96.
"You are the ocean born at once; first, by means of the *vyṛddhi* [vowel].
Thus the syllables (*varṇas*) should be employed; there is no doubt that they are heavy (*guru*) in this case. They know [these] to be the *abhinīta*, the *nipāta*, the *jātya*, or the *svarita*.
At the time of recitation, they are indeed as follows, according to the sequence at the time of reading:
"tava vāyo maho agne vṛṇīmahe"—herein it is seen that the first [syllable] is to be known as light (laghu) and the second as heavy (guru). 98–99.

These twelve names and likewise the deities— if one does not know the correct recitation, one goes to hell otherwise. The *chāyā*, the *chidra*, the *chandas*, and the letter *cha* are designated as "light" (*laghu*).
Whether they be short or long, the remaining [consonants] are established in doubling (dvitva).
According to the injunctions of the scriptures, one should understand that a doubled syllable occurs both before a long vowel and likewise before a short vowel. 101–102.
O Giriśa, that which is long at the beginning, as well as that which is heavy with armor, should be understood as such; I provide this illustration.
Let not the *yājñavalkya* verses, along with the *sahastoma* hymns, [confuse you].
In the middle of a recitation, when three short syllables occur together, they become long at the time of the *padapāṭha*.
(104) From that sacrifice, [the syllable] ending with the *paśus* and the *yajus* formulas is likewise obtained;
however, the letter *cha* does not occur after half a *ṛc*, nor ever in a triple conjunction (*trisamyoga*). (105)

The letter *ṛ* is said to be soft when it does not undergo conjunction or doubling; Śaunaka declared that one should know it to be heavy at the end of a word. A particle (*nipāta*) and a protracted vowel (*abhinīta*) are likewise [heavy], while the remainder is progressively lower in pitch.
One should know that as having three accents; the Hotṛ priest is the manifestation of vigor (ojas).
There are two *k* sounds and two vowels, and no *mātrā* is prescribed. One should apply a counter-accent (*pratisvara*) to each vowel; the *vreśīnām* is the illustration thereof. 107–108.
First a sentence of fourteen syllables, then again one of eleven syllables,
then another of ten syllables, and after that one of eight syllables; yet if it is devoid of the one hundred and eight characteristics, it is like food without condiment.
Thus the phonemes (varṇas) are to be employed; Śrī and they [the phonemes] are the illustration.
A sentence consisting of eight syllables, whether in three lines or four lines—Gāyatrī indeed had seven faces—"Agni, messenger, hear my call"—is the example. 110–111.
One should know that both consist of seven syllables, and again nine syllables;
one should recognize the eight-syllable [verse] which designates the Puruṣa. Thus, these eighty-one syllables have been proclaimed.
These twelve sentences, beginning with the single-syllable one, are twelve in number.
(113) The first consists of twelve syllables; in the fifth there are five and seven [syllables];
then the sentence of six syllables, and again the one remembered as having twelve. (114)
They say it has eleven syllables, and at the end, twelve syllables;
thus the phonemes are to be employed—this is the view expressed by "atha etān.
The eighteen-syllable sentence is fivefold upon the vault of heaven.
The *vaiśvadevī* meter is illustrated by seventeen syllables (116).
Then, with the hundred *kaṇḍikās* following the *raudrādhyāya*,
one should compose a statement consisting of sixteen syllables in half a verse (117).
The eighteen-syllable mantra is again [recited] with sixteen auspicious [syllables];
thus the phonemes should be employed, and one should assign the "strength from the stone" (aśmann ūrjam).

What is studied with wisdom in the presence of the Guru is truly studied; that which is not so is not studied at all. 118. In the book [it is said]: "That which is studied through wisdom is not [merely] studied in the presence of the Guru."
They do not shine in the assembly, like women who have conceived by a paramour.
No single person knows everything, and no one person perceives everything;
thus, the secret counsels of wise men who possess pure intentions are not revealed.
Having heard of the destruction of the Vedas, a wise man should certainly not speak of it directly; rather, having summoned him to a private place, he should speak so that his dharma is not lost.
A mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, when incorrectly employed, does not convey its intended meaning.
That vajra of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [did] due to an error in the accent;
therefore, a wise person should not abandon the defining characteristics, otherwise the tradition would be corrupted. 122.

Without the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the disciple’s tradition is subject to destruction; he who does not know the correct recitation does not attain that fruit. One who knows the defining characteristic is the best, while one who knows the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) is middling. (123–124)
The knower of both the object of definition and the defining characteristic declares that [reality] to be mere consciousness;
Just as speech is devoid of melody and women are without clothing, so too do the letters lack luster when they are devoid of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having thus reflected thoroughly, the student of the Veda should always recite them again in this manner. 126–127.
"Viśvārūpāṇy abodhy agniḥ," "edho 'si," and likewise "ketuṃ kṛṇvan"— these are remembered as the ṣakāra-mantras with hair on their heads (mūrddhaja).
"agner anīkam" is the first, and "yukṣvā hi viśve devāḥ" is the second.
"O Agni, come here"—this is the next [verse]; "I bow down to the one worthy of praise"—this is [the next].

(129) "The divine *barhis*," "when the waters," "you exist today," "well-being for us," and likewise "may he protect us"—these are the [verses] beginning with *mitra*, which proceed with the syllable *kṣa*. (130) Thus they are joined.
Thus ends the Amoghānandinī Śikṣā; now begins the second part of the Amoghānandinī Śikṣā,
the initial verses.
Having bowed my head to Sthāṇu, the Lord of the three worlds,
the three-eyed one, the destroyer of Tripura, and the embodiment of the three Vedas, I shall perform this instruction according to my understanding of the Yajurveda, by the grace of Someśvara.
In this work, which contains illustrative examples from the Mādhyandina recension,
that which is not directly available from the grammatical systems of Pāṇini and others is stated by me in its entirety for the instruction of my students.
The *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, the *nāsikya*s, as well as the *yama*s,
the *jihvāmūlīya*, and the *upadhmānīya*— these nine are dependent on others (*parāśraya*). They are to be known as the *ayogavāha*s, being devoid of their own inherent vowels.
These are the constituent parts of the former; the vowels among these are as before.
These are the final verses.
And when a doubt arises regarding a division, the determination shall be made from the defining characteristics.
The defining characteristic [of the Veda] is not subject to destruction, though its tradition may perish.
Having heard the Veda according to the prescribed rules, one who explains it correctly is indeed wise; by summoning such a teacher to recite it, the Dharma is not lost. 52–53.
"Thinking, 'One person does not know everything; one person does not find everything,' the wise who possess pure intentions are not deluded.
(54) He who, out of delusion, desires to refute a statement that conforms to valid means of knowledge—
That foolish-minded man himself scatters dust against the wind.
Whatever I have done here otherwise than it should be, due to my childish intellect, the learned should correct that accordingly; for who, being an agent, does not become deluded? (55–56)
For this [work], which follows the *lakṣya* (the actual usage), has been composed for the Vājasaneyins;
known as the *Amoghānandinī*, it is to be honored by the wise. 57.
Thus ends the *Amoghānandinī Śikṣā*.
